messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Suresh, a 53-year-old South Asian man married to his high school sweetheart, worked as a painter in a bustling city. However, his life was forever altered by an experience he had during a brief visit to a war-torn region where he was born and raised. The trauma of being caught in the crossfire of a violent conflict left him with deep scars that continue to affect his daily life. The event itself was seared into Suresh's memory: He vividly recalled the acrid smell of smoke, the deafening explosion that shattered nearby buildings, and the feeling of utter helplessness as he tried to shield himself from the chaos. These details had become potent triggers in his current life. The smell of burning rubber or gasoline could instantly transport him back to that horrific moment, sending waves of anxiety through his body. Any loud bang, like fireworks on New Year’s Eve, would cause him to freeze and scan his surroundings for threats. Suresh's daily routine became a series of constant hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors. His body was always tense, ready to react to danger at the slightest provocation. The sound of a car backfiring or even a door slamming shut could send him into an immediate state of alarm, causing his heart rate to spike and his palms to sweat. In response to these triggers, Suresh adopted several maladaptive strategies. He found himself constantly ruminating on why the event happened to him, replaying every detail in his mind and questioning if there was something he could have done differently to prevent it. To cope with this rumination, he threw himself into work, staying busy to avoid thoughts of the traumatic experience. Suresh would often stay late at the job site, painting until well past normal working hours, just to keep his mind occupied. Additionally, Suresh began avoiding news reports about events similar to what happened to him. He no longer watched TV or read newspapers that might contain any reminders of war zones or explosions. This avoidance had consequences both personally and professionally. His wife noticed a significant decrease in their interactions as he withdrew into his work, spending less time engaging with her or participating in family activities. Suresh's negative appraisals about the world around him also began to take hold. He felt that nothing in his life was meaningful anymore, questioning whether he could ever return to the life and identity of a painter. The sense of being no longer capable of doing the things that defined him weighed heavily on him. His belief that the world is inherently dangerous further compounded his hypervigilance and avoidance. The grief Suresh felt when recalling the event was overwhelming, often leaving him in tears. The memory seemed so extreme to him that he sometimes doubted whether it actually happened to him. This made it difficult for him to fully process and integrate what had occurred. It was these feelings of isolation and helplessness that finally pushed Suresh to seek professional help. He was most afraid of losing the meaningful aspects of his life, including his identity as a painter and his connection with his family. What he hoped for was to regain some sense of control over his life, to find a way to coexist with the memories without them overwhelming him. In therapy sessions, Suresh shared that his primary motivation for seeking help was to rebuild his life and reconnect with his wife and work. He longed to return to painting not just as a job but as a source of joy and purpose in his life. The road ahead would require addressing the triggers, managing hypervigilance, and working through the negative appraisals that had taken root in his mind.
